newsitem.title: UK: British court rules in favour of Spanish fishermen.
newsitem.headline: British court rules in favour of Spanish fishermen.

text.p: Spanish fishermen barred from British waters can claim compensation that could run into millions of pounds (dollars), London's High Court ruled on Thursday.
Spanish flag-of-convenience ships were excluded from trawling off Britain from April 1989 to November 1990 after locals complained about the increased competition.

But the European Court of Justice said in a landmark case that the Spaniards were illegally banned and could recover damages. It was the first time a British act of parliament had been overruled by Euro-judges.

Led by Factortame Ltd, 97 owners and managers of vessels, mostly trawlers, obtained a declaration from the London court that British breaches of European law "were sufficiently serious to give rise to liability for any damage that may subsequently be shown to have been caused to the applicants".
The court said the Spaniards were entitled "in principle" to compensation, financed by British taxpayers, but could not claim so-called exemplary damages to punish the government for the breaches.
The British government said it would study the High Court ruling before deciding whether to appeal.
"We're disappointed with the judgement but we're pleased that the court recognised that the United Kingdom acted in good faith," said a Fishing Ministry spokesman.

"It will be for individual applicants to detail their claims but the judgement will not affect measures that we propose to take to ensure that all British fishing vessels have a genuine economic link with the U.K."

The long-running fishing dispute -- with legal wrangling from London to Luxembourg -- has heightened resentment in Britain towards European Union (EU) directives and provoked heated debate in parliament.
So-called quota-hopping became a big problem in the 1980s, when foreigners bought licences covering about a quarter of the British fishing fleet so they could fish British waters.

But they were foiled by a British shipping law that imposed strict nationality and residential requirements on fishermen, forcing nearly 100 Spanish firms, which had set up front companies in Britain so they could fish in British waters, to tie up their boats.

The Spanish estimate each boat lost 350,000 ($570,000) to 500,000 pounds because of the government's unlawful action. The Ministry spokesman could give no details about the likely cost to taxpayers of the claims.
